 Sign In NEWS Diesel gets major November relief as petrol prices edge lower
 FUEL PRICES
 Ashley Lechman 
 05 NOV 2026, 04:45 5 min read Petrol prices fell by 1c a litre from 4 November, while diesel prices dropped by up to R1.20. Picture: AI South African Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana 's announcement of fuel levy reductions in the 2026 Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement (MTBPS) has given petrol users a slight reprieve in fuel prices, while diesel users will enjoy a more substantial decrease. 
 Petrol 93 and 95 will both decrease by 1 cent per litre, while diesel with 0.05% sulphur content falls by R1.10 per litre and 0.005% sulphur diesel by R1.20 per litre.
 Illuminating paraffin and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) prices, however, have been increased. 
 The Minister of Mineral and Petroleum Resources Gwede Mantashe said the adjustments were based on international and local factors, including higher crude oil prices, increased international petroleum product prices and a weaker rand against the United States (US) dollar.
 The department said the average Brent crude oil price increased from $101 to $108 a barrel during the period under review. This was attributed to uncertainty linked to the conflict in the Middle East , including recent attacks on Saudi Arabian infrastructure, as well as higher freight and insurance costs associated with ship-to-ship transfers. 
 The department said prices for middle distillates were affected by tight global supply, higher seasonal demand ahead of winter in the northern hemisphere and the continuing Russia-Ukraine conflict.
 These increases came despite efforts by the G7 to improve global diesel supply, the US waiving certain Russia sanctions and Russia lifting export restrictions.
 The higher international product prices added 80.41 cents per litre to the basic fuel price of petrol, 94.22 cents per litre to diesel and 225.23 cents per litre to illuminating paraffin.
 The rand also weakened against the US dollar, depreciating from an average of R16.21 to R16.55 during the period.
 This contributed to increases in the basic fuel price of 36.93 cents per litre for petrol, 49 cents for diesel and 49.26 cents for illuminating paraffin.
 Another factor affecting the fuel price structure is the slate levy, which has increased from 87.66 cents to 135.84 cents per litre.
 The department said the cumulative slate balance for petrol and diesel stood at a negative R15.876 billion at the end of September.
 Neil Roets , CEO of Debt Rescue, said that from a consumer affordability perspective, the November fuel adjustment provided welcome relief, but it needed to be viewed against the much broader pressure households had faced over recent months. 
 "For petrol users, the 1 cent per litre decrease is effectively negligible. With inland 95 petrol still above R30 per litre, motorists already dealing with high transport, food and electricity costs are unlikely to feel any meaningful improvement in their monthly budgets," Roets said.  
 "The diesel reduction of between R1.10 and R1.20 per litre is more significant, particularly because diesel costs influence logistics, agriculture, public transport and the movement of goods. However, the reduction needs context. After falling earlier in the year, diesel prices climbed sharply over the past few months. Even after November’s decrease, Gauteng 0.005% diesel remains around R6.43 per litre, or approximately 25%, higher than its July figure," Roets said.  
 The department confirmed the following adjustments for November: 
 • Petrol 93: decrease of 1 cent per litre.
• Petrol 95: decrease of 1 cent per litre.
• Diesel 0.05% sulphur: decrease of 109.82 cents per litre.
• Diesel 0.005% sulphur: decrease of 119.82 cents per litre.
• Wholesale illuminating paraffin: increase of R2.75 per litre.
• Single Maximum National Retail Price for illuminating paraffin: increase of R3.66 per litre.
• LPG: increase of R1.83 per kilogram, with an increase of R2.08 per kilogram in the Western Cape.
 "I see the November diesel decrease as genuine relief, but not yet a reversal of the broader fuel-cost burden consumers and businesses have absorbed. Importantly, government’s temporary reduction in the general fuel levy has played a significant role in protecting consumers from an even more severe adjustment. Without that intervention, households would have faced a substantially larger increase at the pumps this month," Roets added.  
 He said that it should not be underestimated. 
 At a time when household budgets are already stretched, preventing an additional fuel-price shock has real value. The intervention has absorbed part of an external cost increase that would otherwise have landed directly on consumers and businesses. 
 "The challenge is that this protection is temporary. Government can soften the impact of extraordinary international conditions for a limited period, but it cannot permanently insulate South Africans from sustained international oil-price pressure. That remains the underlying risk. Oil prices are still elevated and volatile, while movements in the rand continue to influence the local fuel price," Roets said.  
 The Debt Rescue CEO said that, in his experience, working with financially distressed consumers, it is often the cumulative effect of repeated increases in unavoidable expenses that causes the greatest difficulty. 
 "Households can cut discretionary spending only so far. November should therefore not be dismissed as insignificant. Government intervention has helped prevent a considerably worse outcome, and the diesel reduction offers genuine relief. But household affordability has not recovered, and consumers remain highly exposed to persistently high fuel costs," Roets said.
